The other natural reading (2% of annual margin = 480,000 is the pre-detection cost of an incident) gives a saving of 24M x 0.02 x (1 - 3/42) = about 445,700 per incident, roughly 9x larger, and flips the ranking. The answer states its reading but never shows the sensitivity to it, although it is the assumption the data least pin down and the question asks for sensitivity to the least-trusted assumptions. Also 51,400 is inconsistent with the other rounded figures (55,400 - 3,900 = 51,500; unrounded 51,439).

'Easy to miss' is not general: 0.2 sd is a z-score above 10 at the 7,200 rows/day the answer itself uses for B, so a sensitive test would flag it every day; it is missed only when seasonal swings (weekend about 17% above the pool) and tolerance are of similar size. Also the offset persists, so it can be mistaken for a stable level difference.
'Higher' is ambiguous: higher than C's 7-day pool (4 days of rows vs 7), but lower than B's single day.

perturb receives a live view of X[:, col]. A perturb function that works in place (c *= -1; return c) mutates the caller's evaluation matrix, then X2 and X are identical and the check silently passes with 0 failures (reproduced: 50 rows, 0 failures, X mutated). This contradicts the answer's own 'never mutate the evaluation set in place' and 'a test that can never fail' warnings.
Same change so the fenced code equals code.solution.

Overstated as worded: if the stolen identity can also launch pipeline jobs, the pipeline identity will register whatever that code produces (including a pickle with a payload), so the token can still get a malicious artifact to the approval step. Production is then protected only by the approval and the integrity/loader controls, which the answer covers only generically. Also experiment-namespace artifacts remain a lateral-movement path between notebooks.
The rubric point (and a useful control) is alerting on production-alias moves; the answer's audit item describes only a passive log.

'Adding noise to outputs' is grouped with DP training and then covered by 'the strongest option'. Output noise that leaves the label unchanged is confidence masking, which label-only attacks defeat (the answer says so two bullets earlier). Only DP training (and, per the same paper, strong L2 regularisation) stopped all attacks tested.

Warm start is path dependent: its risks (forgetting, error persistence) accumulate over consecutive updates. Sampling 10-15 isolated origin days tests only single-step warm starts from a fresh checkpoint, hides exactly the failure modes the answer lists, and makes the 'day-to-day stability' and 'injected bad batch recovery' checks impossible. The warm-start chain is cheap (about 40 min per day), only the full-retrain baseline needs sampling.
Vague and unsourced; the meaning is unclear to a grader
The full-retrain baseline is run only on a sample of days, so stability can be compared only for the warm-start chain (or between sampled days).
